summary: Supply amount of options you will trade and the strike price of the put you buy (The put you buy (long put)) and the Options spread calculator solves for net debit spread. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Options spread calculator work?
sections.html:
The Options spread calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports net debit spread in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select calculator mode); then you type in amount of options you will trade, the strike price of the put you buy (The put you buy (long put)), the net debit spread (Bull call estimated returns) and the maximum loss (Bull call estimated returns).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Options spread calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Premium received for selling the call=premium spent for buying the call + net debit spread ÷ amount of options you will trade
Premium spent for buying the call=-1 ÷ 100 × maximum loss ÷ amount of options you will trade + premium received for selling the call
Premium spent for buying the call=-1 ÷ 100 × maximum profit ÷ amount of options you will trade + premium received for selling the call − strike price of the call you buy + strike price of the call you sell
Premium spent for buying the call=breakeven price + premium received for selling the call − strike price of the call you buy
Premium spent for buying the call=-1 ÷ 100 × potential profit ÷ amount of options you will trade + premium received for selling the call − strike price of the call you buy + your target price at expiration
Premium spent for buying the put=-net credit spread ÷ amount of options you will trade + premium received for selling the put

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Select calculator mode set to Bull call spread, Amount of options you will trade = 10, Premium spent for buying the call = 10 and Net debit spread = 10. The calculator returns Premium received for selling the call = 11 and Maximum loss = 1000.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Premium received for selling the call = 11 and Maximum loss = 1000 should be roughly the size you expected from Select calculator mode set to Bull call spread and Amount of options you will trade = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Options spread calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — amount of options you will trade and the strike price of the put you buy (The put you buy (long put)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Options spread calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns net debit spread, derived from amount of options you will trade and the strike price of the put you buy (The put you buy (long put)). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Options spread calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for amount of options you will trade and the strike price of the put you buy (The put you buy (long put)), which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your target price at expiration in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your target price at expiration opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Premium received for selling the call = 11. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Options spread calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
